source_text: Plane monet Romanos omnibus potestatibus subjici, quia non sit potestas nisi a Deo, quia non sine caussa gladium gestet, et quia ministerium sit Dei; sed et ultrix, inquit, in iram ei qui malum fecerit. Nam et praemiserat: Principes enim non sunt timori bono operi, sed malo. Vis autem non timere potestatem? fac bonum, et laudem ab ea referes. Dei ergo ministra est tibi in bonum. Si vero malum facias, time. Ita, non in occasione frustrandi martyrii jubet te subjici potestatibus, sed in provocatione bene vivendi, etiam sub illarum respectu, quasi adjutricum justitiae, quasi ministrarum divini judicii, hic etiam de nocentibus praejudicantis. Dehinc et exequitur quomodo velit te subjici potestatibus, reddere jubens, cui tributum, tributum; cui vectigal, vectigal; id est quae sunt Caesaris, Caesari, et quae Dei, Deo; solius autem Dei homo. Condixerat scilicet Petrus, regem quidem honorandum; ut tamen tunc rex honoretur, cum suis rebus insistit, cum a divinis honoribus longe est; quia et pater et mater diligentur, cum Deo non comparabuntur. Caeterum, super Deum diligi nec animam licebit.
pass_a_gloss: It clearly warns Romans to be subject to all powers, because there is no power except from God, because he does not bear the sword without cause, and because it is a ministry of God; but also avenging, it says, in wrath to him who has done evil. For it had also sent ahead: For rulers are not a terror to good work, but to evil. Do you want not to fear power? Do good, and you will receive praise from it. Therefore, it is a minister of God to you for good. If indeed you do evil, fear. Thus, not on the occasion of frustrating martyrdom does it order you to be subject to powers, but in the provocation of living well, even under their regard, as if a helper of justice, as if a minister of divine judgment, here also prejudging concerning those who do harm. Next, it also follows how it wants you to be subject to powers, ordering to render, to whom tribute, tribute; to whom tax, tax; that is, the things that are Caesar's, to Caesar, and the things that are God's, to God; but man is of God alone. Certainly, Peter had agreed, that a king is to be honored; yet the king is to be honored only when he stands by his own things, when he is far from divine honors; because also a father and a mother are loved, when they will not be compared to God. Moreover, to love more than God is not permitted, neither the soul.

choices.why: feminine form of ulterior, meaning avenging or punishing
feminine form of minister, referring to the power as a servant of God

choices.english: but man is of God alone
choices.why: emphasizing the unique relationship between God and humanity
introducing a contrasting or additional idea
indicating the superiority of God's love

pass_b_english: He bluntly warns the Romans to submit to every authority, because no authority exists except from God, because the ruler does not carry the sword for nothing, and because it is a ministry of God—but also an avenger, he says, bringing wrath on the one who does evil (Romans 13:1-7). Scripture had already laid the groundwork: rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to evil. You want to stop fearing authority? Do good, and you will win its praise. So it is God’s servant for your good. But if you do evil, be afraid. Therefore, the command to submit is not given to sabotage martyrdom, but to provoke good living even under their gaze, as if they were assistants of justice, ministers of divine judgment, here already passing preliminary sentence on wrongdoers. He then spells out what that submission looks like: pay what you owe—tribute to whom tribute is due, tax to whom tax is due; that is, render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s (Matthew 22:21); the human person belongs to God alone. Peter had agreed that a king deserves honor, yet a king is honored only when he stays in his lane, keeping his distance from divine honors; a father and mother are loved precisely because they are not equated with God. Beyond that, loving anything more than God is not permitted—not even your own soul.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass B correctly identifies and adds the necessary scripture citations (Romans 13:1-7 and Matthew 22:21) for the alluded passages, which is required by the instructions. The nuances of 'solius autem Dei homo' and the conditional nature of honoring kings are preserved.
